title: The Three Domains
description: How life sorts into Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya

concepts.title: Bacteria — Workhorses and Pathogens
concepts.contentHtml:
Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes — no nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles. Most are 0.5-5 μm across.

They live everywhere: in soil, water, our gut, on our skin. Of the ~4 × 10¹³ bacterial cells associated with a human body, only a small fraction are pathogens. The rest digest our food, train our immune system, and exclude harmful invaders.

Bacteria reproduce by binary fission — a single cell can split every 20 minutes under good conditions, doubling exponentially.

concepts.title: Archaea — Extremophiles and More
concepts.contentHtml:
Archaea look like bacteria but are biochemically distinct — different cell membrane lipids, different ribosomes, different metabolisms. Their molecular biology often resembles eukaryotes more than bacteria.

Many are extremophiles: thermophiles in hot springs (>100 °C), halophiles in saturated salt, methanogens in oxygen-free environments. Methanogens in wetlands, rice paddies, cattle and termites produce nearly all of the world's biological methane.

Recent research shows archaea are also abundant in mild environments — in soil, oceans, and the human microbiome.

concepts.title: Fungi — Decomposers, Symbionts, Pathogens
concepts.contentHtml:
Fungi are eukaryotes — yeasts (single-celled like Saccharomyces) and molds and mushrooms (multicellular). Cell walls of chitin (not cellulose).

Fungi decompose dead organic matter, returning nutrients to soil. Mycorrhizal fungi associate with ~90% of plant roots, exchanging nutrients for sugars. Yeasts ferment our beer, bread, and wine.

Pathogenic fungi (Candida, Aspergillus, Cryptococcus) cause major human disease, especially in immunocompromised patients. Antifungal drugs are limited — fungi share enough biology with us that drugs often have side effects.

concepts.title: Cell Wall and Gram Staining
concepts.contentHtml:
Most bacteria have a peptidoglycan cell wall — a mesh of sugar chains crosslinked by peptide bonds.

Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall (e.g., Staphylococcus, Streptococcus). They retain the crystal violet dye in Gram staining and appear purple.

Gram-negative bacteria have a thin wall sandwiched between two membranes (e.g., E. coli, Pseudomonas). They lose the violet dye and pick up the counterstain (safranin), appearing pink.

The distinction matters clinically — antibiotics often target one group preferentially. Gram-negatives are usually more resistant due to the outer membrane.

concepts.title: DNA & Plasmids
concepts.contentHtml:
Bacterial DNA is typically a single circular chromosome floating in the cytoplasm — no nucleus.

Many bacteria also carry small accessory DNA molecules called plasmids. Plasmids often encode useful (to the bacterium) traits: antibiotic resistance, toxin production, the ability to metabolize unusual nutrients.

Plasmids can be transferred between bacteria via conjugation (a kind of bacterial mating). This is one major mechanism of antibiotic resistance spread.

concepts.title: Antibiotics
concepts.contentHtml:
Antibiotics kill or inhibit bacteria selectively — exploiting differences between bacterial and human cells.

Penicillin blocks peptidoglycan crosslinking — bacterial cell walls weaken and burst osmotically. Tetracyclines and macrolides bind bacterial ribosomes (different from ours). Fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase. Each targets a difference.

Antibiotic resistance is the existential challenge: bacteria evolve, plasmids spread, our pipeline of new antibiotics has stagnated. Stewardship and new drug discovery are urgent.

concepts.title: Who Lives on Us?
concepts.contentHtml:
The average human carries roughly 4 × 10¹³ bacterial cells, about as many as our own ~3 × 10¹³ human cells. (The old claim of ten bacteria per human cell was revised down by a 2016 census.)

The bulk live in the gut. Skin, mouth, nose, and reproductive tract host their own distinct communities. Each body site has its characteristic microbiota.

Modern sequencing (16S rRNA, shotgun metagenomics) has cataloged thousands of species, many of which haven't been cultured in the lab. The microbiome is a vast unexplored frontier.

concepts.title: What the Microbiome Does
concepts.contentHtml:
Gut bacteria digest fibers we can't (producing short-chain fatty acids that feed our gut cells), synthesize vitamins (B12, K, biotin), and exclude pathogens through competition.

The microbiome trains and modulates our immune system. Children raised without normal microbial exposure have higher rates of allergies and autoimmune disease.

Microbiome composition correlates with obesity, depression, autism risk, and response to cancer immunotherapy. Causation is harder to establish — much remains unsettled.

concepts.title: Manipulating the Microbiome
concepts.contentHtml:
Probiotics (live bacteria) and prebiotics (nutrients that feed beneficial bacteria) aim to shift microbiome composition. Evidence for specific health benefits is mixed.

Fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) is dramatic and effective for recurrent C. difficile infections. Trials are exploring it for IBD, autism, and metabolic disease.

Designer microbiome therapies — defined consortia of bacteria, engineered probiotics — are an emerging field. The microbiome is becoming pharmacology.

concepts.title: Metabolic Diversity
concepts.contentHtml:
Microbes have vastly more metabolic diversity than animals or plants. They can use nearly any organic molecule (and many inorganic ones) as energy sources, with various electron acceptors.

Aerobes use O₂. Anaerobes use NO₃⁻, SO₄²⁻, Fe³⁺, or even CO₂ as terminal electron acceptors. Some grow chemolithotrophically — eating rocks (oxidizing reduced sulfur, iron, ammonia) for energy.

Photoautotrophs (cyanobacteria, photosynthetic bacteria) use light + CO₂. Each metabolic strategy has its niche.

concepts.title: Microbial Biogeochemistry
concepts.contentHtml:
Microbes drive Earth's elemental cycles. The nitrogen cycle — fixation of N₂ to NH₃ (only some bacteria/archaea can do this), nitrification (NH₃ → NO₃⁻), denitrification (NO₃⁻ → N₂) — is almost entirely microbial.

Sulfur cycle: H₂S ↔ S° ↔ SO₄²⁻, mostly via microbial transformations. Carbon cycle: photosynthesis fixes; respiration releases; methanogens add CH₄.

Modern climate models include microbial fluxes — they're not optional details. Soil microbes alone respire ~60 Gt C/year globally.

concepts.title: Microbiomes in Ecosystems
concepts.contentHtml:
Soil teems with microbes — billions per gram. They drive decomposition, nutrient cycling, plant nutrition (mycorrhizae, nitrogen-fixing rhizobia).

Ocean microbes are major actors in the global carbon cycle: marine photosynthesis is comparable in scale to terrestrial. Picocyanobacteria like Prochlorococcus contribute ~5% of global photosynthesis.

Hot vents, deep subsurface, glacier ice — wherever you look, microbes are there. They are the biosphere's foundation.

concepts.title: Fermentation & Industrial Production
concepts.contentHtml:
Microbial fermentation has been making bread, beer, wine, cheese, and yogurt for millennia. Industrial fermentation now produces antibiotics, vitamins, amino acids, enzymes (rennet, amylases), and bulk chemicals (ethanol, lactic acid).

Aerobic fermentation in bioreactors of thousands of cubic meters drives major sectors of the chemical industry — and it's increasingly competitive with petrochemistry.

concepts.title: Recombinant Production
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1970s recombinant DNA revolution transformed microbial biotech. Insert a human gene into E. coli or yeast, and the microbes produce human proteins.

Insulin (1982 — first recombinant drug), human growth hormone, interferons, vaccines, monoclonal antibodies. Major fractions of the modern pharmaceutical industry rely on engineered microbes.

CHO (Chinese hamster ovary) cells supplement microbial production for proteins requiring complex glycosylation, but bacteria and yeast still dominate where they suffice.

concepts.title: Synthetic Biology
concepts.contentHtml:
Synthetic biology goes beyond expressing single genes — it engineers entire genetic circuits and metabolic pathways.

Artemisinin (antimalarial) was produced industrially from 2013 via engineered yeast, though the process proved uneconomic against plant-derived supply. Bacteria have been programmed to compute logic operations, count divisions, and produce complex aromatics.

Frontiers: minimal genomes (Mycoplasma JCVI-syn3.0), tagged organisms with new genetic codes, environmental sensors that release drugs only when conditions match. Microbes are programmable matter.
